lead: Engine testing turns a running engine into numbers: power delivered, fuel burnt, heat lost. This unit shows how each of those numbers is measured, how the measurements combine into efficiencies, and why two tests of the same engine can give different results. After it you can compute brake and indicated power, close a heat balance, and read a test report or a pressure-crank angle record without help.
about: The unit turns an engine on a test bed into numbers you can compare. It starts with the measured quantities (torque, brake power, mean effective pressure, specific fuel consumption) and the efficiencies built from them, then separates indicated, brake and friction power, shows how fuel and air flow are measured, and covers the dynamometers and test cells that load the engine. The heat balance closes the energy account. The last three chapters list the variables that move every one of these numbers, the standard ways to push performance up, and the test standards, driving cycles and in-cylinder pressure measurement that make two engines comparable.

chapters.idea: Every performance figure is a ratio or a product of three measurable things: torque, speed and fuel flow.
chapters.depth: Define each term before using it: torque T (N·m), speed N (rev/s), brake power BP = 2πNT/60, indicated power IP, friction power FP = IP − BP, mechanical efficiency η_mech = BP/IP. Mean effective pressure is a fictitious constant pressure acting on the piston for the whole stroke: bmep = 2π n_R T / V_d, where n_R = 2 for a four-stroke and 1 for a two-stroke and V_d is the swept volume in m³. Give brake thermal efficiency, indicated thermal efficiency, BSFC and ISFC, volumetric efficiency, relative efficiency, equivalence ratio, specific power per litre and per kg. Some syllabi call these 'performance characteristics' and ask for the shape of the BP, BSFC and η curves against speed and load. Keep the four-stroke factor n_R visible in every formula.

figure.title: How three measurements give every performance number
figure.aria: Block diagram: measured torque and speed give brake power, measured fuel flow and calorific value give fuel power, and brake thermal efficiency is the ratio of the two.

chapters.example: A single-cylinder four-stroke engine has bore 100 mm and stroke 120 mm. At 1500 rpm it holds a bmep of 6 bar and burns 2.4 kg/h of fuel of calorific value 43 MJ/kg. Mechanical efficiency is 85 %. Find swept volume, brake power, torque, brake thermal efficiency, BSFC, indicated power and friction power. Answers: V_d = 9.425 × 10⁻⁴ m³ (0.9425 L); BP = 7.07 kW; T = 45.0 N·m; fuel power = 28.67 kW; η_bth = 24.7 %; BSFC = 339.5 g/kWh; IP = 8.32 kW; FP = 1.25 kW.
chapters.trap: Forgetting the 2 in N/2 for a four-stroke, or putting rpm into 2πNT/60 without dividing by 60. Also mixing bar with Pa, and quoting BSFC in g/kWh in a formula that needs kg/kWh.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: engine terminology, swept volume, four-stroke and two-stroke working cycles.
chapters.leave: Air-standard and fuel-air cycle analysis (Unit 1); formation of pollutants (Unit 6).

chapters.idea: Brake power is measured directly, but indicated and friction power must be separated by a test that removes one cylinder or one source of loss at a time.
chapters.depth: Indicated power from an indicator diagram: take the p-V loop, measure its area with a planimeter or by counting squares, divide by the diagram length to get imep, then apply imep = IP × 60 /(V_d × N/n_R). Mention the old mechanical indicator card and the modern piezoelectric route to the same p-V loop. Brake power from dynamometer torque and speed. Friction power by three routes: Morse test on multi-cylinder engines — cut one cylinder at a time and treat the drop in brake power as that cylinder's indicated power; motoring test — drive the engine with a dynamometer (fuel and ignition off) and take the motoring power as FP; Willan's line — plot fuel flow against BP at constant speed and extrapolate the straight part back to zero fuel flow, the intercept on the fuel axis being the friction loss. State the assumptions of each: FP stays constant with load, the firing cylinders do not change when one is cut, and the Willan line is straight. Give the drawbacks that examiners ask for: Morse test needs a multi-cylinder engine, motoring gives cold-engine friction, Willan's line fails at very light load.

figure.title: Three routes to the three powers

nodes.label: Morse test
nodes.note: cut one cylinder at a time

figure.aria: Block diagram: dynamometer torque gives brake power, the Morse test gives indicated power, and friction power is the difference of the two.

chapters.example: Morse test on a four-cylinder engine running at constant speed. Brake power with all four cylinders firing is 20.0 kW. Cutting cylinders 1, 2, 3 and 4 in turn gives 14.2, 14.0, 14.3 and 14.1 kW. Find indicated power, friction power and mechanical efficiency. Drops are 5.8, 6.0, 5.7 and 5.9 kW, so IP = 23.4 kW, FP = 20.0 − 23.4, that is FP = 23.4 − 20.0 = 3.4 kW, and η_mech = 20.0/23.4 = 85.5 %.
chapters.trap: Adding the four cut readings instead of the four drops. Each drop BP − BP_i is that cylinder's indicated power. Also: FP must come out small and positive, so a negative FP means the arithmetic or the reading is wrong.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 for the power and efficiency definitions; Unit 1 for the working cycle.
chapters.leave: Dynamometer construction and test cell layout (5.4); heat release analysis from the same pressure record (Unit 3).

chapters.idea: Power means nothing without knowing how much fuel and air produced it, so both flows are measured at the same time as the load.
chapters.depth: Fuel: volumetric method with a burette and stopwatch, gravimetric method with a weighing balance and stopwatch, and continuous meters (rotameter, turbine, Coriolis). Convert volume to mass using density; mf in kg/h = (volume in L × density in kg/L × 3600) ÷ time in s. Say why a small burette and a short time give a large error, and how a three-way cock avoids counting the filling time. Air: air-box with a sharp-edged orifice and a U-tube manometer, venturi meter, hot-wire anemometer, and the engine-as-compressor method. Give the orifice relation ma = C_d A √(2 ρ Δp) and the density correction ρ = p/(R T) from the test-room readings. Then air-fuel ratio by mass, and volumetric efficiency η_vol = actual air mass per cycle ÷ (intake density × swept volume). One line on gas fuels measured with a gas meter.

figure.title: Two flows, one ratio
figure.aria: Block diagram: burette timing gives fuel mass flow in kg/h, air box gives air mass flow in kg/s, their ratio is the air-fuel ratio, and air flow against the ideal swept-volume flow gives volumetric efficiency.

chapters.example: A four-cylinder four-stroke engine of 2.0 L runs at 3000 rpm. The air box orifice shows 0.052 kg/s. A burette test uses 50 mL of diesel of density 830 kg/m³ in 25 s. Intake air density is 1.18 kg/m³. Find fuel flow in kg/h, the air-fuel ratio, and the volumetric efficiency. Fuel mass = 0.050 × 0.83 = 0.0415 kg, so mf = 0.0415 × 3600/25 = 5.98 kg/h = 1.66 × 10⁻³ kg/s. AFR = 0.052 ÷ 1.66 × 10⁻³ = 31.3. Ideal air = 1.18 × 2.0 × 10⁻³ × (3000/60)/2 = 0.0590 kg/s, so η_vol = 0.052/0.0590 = 88.1 %.
chapters.trap: Using a volume ratio as the air-fuel ratio — AFR is always by mass. Also forgetting to correct air density for the test-room temperature and pressure, which changes both AFR and volumetric efficiency.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 and 5.2 for the power figures the flows are divided by; Unit 2 for how fuel is delivered to the engine.
chapters.leave: Carburettor and injection hardware (Unit 2); gas analysers and smoke meters (Unit 6).

chapters.idea: A dynamometer is a brake that measures the torque it absorbs, and a test cell is the room that makes that measurement repeatable and safe.
chapters.depth: Absorption dynamometers: Prony brake and rope brake (cheap, simple, poor at high speed, cooling problems), hydraulic or water brake, eddy-current brake, DC generator. Motoring and transient dynamometers: DC and AC machines that can also drive the engine, needed for motoring tests and for following a driving cycle second by second. Torque measurement by a torque arm with a spring balance, a load cell or a strain gauge on the shaft; BP = 2πNT/60 with T = W × L for a simple arm. Test cell: rigid bed and anti-vibration mounts, coupling with guard, fuel and coolant supply, ventilation, exhaust extraction, fire safety, and the instrument panel that logs speed, torque, temperatures and flows. Say what a transient dynamometer does that an absorption one cannot: change speed and load fast enough to follow a city driving cycle.

figure.aria: Tree of dynamometer types: absorption machines load the engine and cannot drive it, while motoring and transient machines can also drive the engine.

chapters.example: A hydraulic dynamometer has a torque arm of 0.5 m and the spring balance reads 120 N at 1500 rpm. Find the torque and the brake power. If the engine is a 1.0 L four-stroke, find the bmep. T = 120 × 0.5 = 60 N·m. BP = 2πNT/60 = 2π × 1500 × 60/60 = 9425 W = 9.42 kW. bmep = 2π n_R T/V_d = 2π × 2 × 60 ÷ 1.0 × 10⁻³ = 7.54 × 10⁵ Pa = 7.54 bar.
chapters.trap: Using the arm diameter instead of the radius, forgetting the dead weight that the balance reads with no load, and putting rpm straight into 2πNT/60. Watch the units of torque arm (metres, not mm).
chapters.prereq: 5.2 for brake power from torque and speed; 5.1 for bmep.
chapters.leave: Standard test procedures and power correction factors (5.8); transient cycle details (5.8).

chapters.idea: Fuel energy must come out somewhere, and the heat balance sheet shows where: brake, cooling water, exhaust, and the rest.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach the heat balance as a full topic. Energy in = fuel power mf × CV. Energy out = brake power + heat to cooling water + heat carried by exhaust gas + unaccounted (radiation, convection, oil cooler, incomplete combustion). Give the measurement of each: water flow rate and temperature rise across the jacket, exhaust gas mass flow and temperature with cp about 1.05 kJ/kgK, and a gas calorimeter if the exhaust is to be checked. Present the sheet in kW and as a percentage of fuel power; the percentages must add to 100 %. Draw it as a bar or a divided block rather than a pie chart with many thin slices. Keep the chapter short: one worked sheet, the four losses, one line on why the unaccounted term shrinks as the engine gets hotter.

figure.title: Heat balance of the worked example
figure.aria: Block diagram of a heat balance: 35 kW of fuel energy leaves as 10 kW brake power, 5.0 kW to cooling water, 18.9 kW in the exhaust and about 1.1 kW unaccounted.

chapters.example: An engine burns 3.0 kg/h of fuel of calorific value 42 MJ/kg and gives 10 kW at the brake. Cooling water flows at 6 kg/min with a 12 °C rise. Exhaust gas flows at 0.045 kg/s with cp = 1.05 kJ/kgK and a 400 K rise. Draw the heat balance in kW and in percent. Fuel power = 3.0 × 42/3.6 = 35 kW. Cooling = (6/60) × 4.18 × 12 = 5.02 kW. Exhaust = 0.045 × 1.05 × 400 = 18.9 kW. Unaccounted = 35 − 10 − 5.02 − 18.9 = 1.08 kW. Percent: 28.6, 14.3, 54.0 and 3.1.
chapters.trap: The sheet must add up to fuel power, not to brake power. Also the exhaust mass flow is air plus fuel, not air alone, and kW must not be mixed with kJ/h on the same sheet.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 for fuel power and brake thermal efficiency; 5.2 and 5.3 for brake power and fuel flow.
chapters.leave: Emission species and their measurement (Unit 6); cooling system hardware (Unit 4).

chapters.idea: Any variable that changes the trapped air mass, the mixture strength or the timing moves power, efficiency and emissions together.
chapters.depth: Go variable by variable and give the shape of the curve, not just a list: speed (friction rises faster than indicated power at high speed, so BSFC has a minimum), load (BSFC lowest around three-quarter load), air-fuel ratio (best power slightly rich, best efficiency lean; equivalence ratio φ), spark or injection timing (maximum brake torque timing, too much advance gives knock and high NOx), compression ratio, intake air temperature and pressure (altitude, weather), humidity, coolant and oil temperature, carbon deposits, valve clearance, exhaust back pressure, fuel quality (octane, cetane, calorific value, density). Say clearly that the standard corrects measured power to reference air conditions, so observed and corrected power are different numbers. One short paragraph linking timing and mixture to CO, HC and NOx, pointing to Unit 6.

figure.aria: Two curves of brake thermal efficiency against speed: the correctly timed engine peaks near 2600 rpm and higher, while a retarded engine peaks earlier and lower.

chapters.example: A naturally aspirated diesel gives 40 kW at 25 °C and 1.00 bar on a standard day. It is retested on a hot afternoon at 40 °C and 0.90 bar. Assuming brake power follows intake air density, find the density ratio and the observed power. Density ratio = (0.90/1.00) × (298/313) = 0.857. Observed power ≈ 40 × 0.857 = 34.3 kW, about 14 % lower, although nothing on the engine was touched.
chapters.trap: Quoting an observed power as the engine's rating. Test standards correct to reference temperature, pressure and humidity, so always state whether the figure is observed or corrected.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 to 5.3 for the measured quantities; Unit 2 for ignition and injection timing; Unit 3 for knock.
chapters.leave: Knock chemistry and flame speed theory (Unit 3); pollutant formation (Unit 6).

chapters.idea: Performance is improved by four levers only: more air, better mixture, less friction, and better control.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this as a separate topic, so keep it a short list with one line of physics each. More air: turbocharging and supercharging (cross-reference Unit 4), intercooling, variable geometry turbine, four valves and better ports, variable valve timing. Better mixture: high-pressure common rail, electronic injection timing, finer spray, better combustion chamber shape. Less friction: low-viscosity lubricants with friction modifiers, surface coatings, lighter reciprocating parts, better piston rings and bearings. Better control: closed-loop ECU with lambda and knock sensors, cylinder deactivation, stop-start. Cycle changes: Miller/Atkinson operation and a higher compression ratio. End with the trade-off: every step that raises power or efficiency usually raises NOx or cost, and must be proved on a standard test.

figure.aria: Tree grouping the ways to improve performance into four families: more air, better mixture, less friction and better control.

chapters.example: A 2.0 L naturally aspirated petrol engine gives 80 kW. A turbocharger with an intercooler raises intake air density to 1.4 times the ambient value. At the same air-fuel ratio and a BSFC of 240 g/kWh, find the new power and the new fuel flow. New power = 80 × 1.4 = 112 kW, a 40 % gain. Fuel flow = 240 g/kWh × 112 kW = 26 880 g/h = 26.9 kg/h, against 19.2 kg/h before.
chapters.trap: Thinking boost alone raises power. Air and fuel must both rise by the same ratio, and the knock limit or turbine inlet temperature sets the ceiling, not the boost number.
chapters.prereq: 5.6 for the variables being pushed; Unit 4 for supercharging and turbocharging.
chapters.leave: Turbocharger construction, turbo lag and intercooler types (Unit 4); emission control and after-treatment (Unit 6).

chapters.idea: A test result is only a result if it follows an agreed procedure, and the in-cylinder pressure record is the most detailed evidence an engine test can give.
chapters.depth: Test standards: what a rated power means — gross or net, with or without fan, alternator and exhaust system, after a defined running-in, at steady state. Power correction to reference air temperature, pressure and humidity, quoting ISO 1585, ISO 3046 and SAE J1349, and the equivalent Indian standard. Emission standards and driving cycles: NEDC, WLTC and the modified Indian driving cycle, and Bharat Stage VI limits. Make the point that the cycle decides the number, so results from two cycles cannot be compared. In-cylinder pressure measurement: piezoelectric transducer (flush mounted, sometimes water cooled), charge amplifier, crank-angle encoder, TDC reference, and pegging the relative piezo signal to the motoring line to get absolute pressure. Then the products of the record: p-θ and p-V plots, imep, peak pressure and the crank angle where it occurs, heat release rate, combustion duration, and cycle-to-cycle variation as the coefficient of variation of imep, COV = (standard deviation ÷ mean) × 100 %.

figure.title: From cylinder to numbers
figure.aria: Block diagram of the pressure measurement chain, from the cylinder through the piezoelectric transducer, charge amplifier and crank-angle data logger to the final imep, peak pressure and cycle-to-cycle variation.

chapters.example: A piezoelectric transducer and crank-angle encoder record 100 cycles of a 1.5 L four-stroke engine at 2000 rpm, imep 8.2 bar, peak pressure 78 bar at 8° ATDC. The mean imep over the 100 cycles is 8.2 bar with a standard deviation of 0.21 bar. Find indicated power and the COV of imep. IP = imep × V_d × (N/60)/2 = 8.2 × 10⁵ × 1.5 × 10⁻³ × 16.67 = 20 500 W = 20.5 kW. COV = (0.21/8.2) × 100 = 2.6 %, well inside the 5 % usually taken as the limit for stable combustion.
chapters.trap: Treating the piezo signal as absolute pressure without pegging it to the motoring line, and ignoring TDC offset: one degree of TDC error moves both peak pressure and imep.
chapters.prereq: 5.2 for imep to indicated power; 5.4 for the test cell; Unit 3 for combustion stages; Unit 6 for emission standards.
chapters.leave: NDIR, flame ionisation detector, chemiluminescence analyser and smoke meters (Unit 6); heat release theory in detail (Unit 3).
